INDEPENDENT STUDY TEXT / EXPANDED TEACHING EDITION
Advanced Quantum
Computing
Mathematics, algorithms and research for Athena
This book bridges introductory quantum computing and the mathematical work needed to derive al-
gorithms. Its destination is a research prototype for Athena, a multi-agent assistant that allocates tasks,
models resources and plans workflows. All explanations, examples, diagrams and exercises here are
newly written; references identify the underlying results.
What to bring. Familiarity with algebra, functions and basic probability is enough to start. Com-
plex linear algebra is developed first. Derivatives and integrals are introduced where needed; full
differential-equation theory is not assumed. Paper, a pencil and patience are suﬀicient for the worked
examples. Code is explanatory pseudocode and does not require a laptop to follow.
How to study. Read one numbered lesson at a time. Before looking at a worked calculation, attempt
the next line yourself. Reproduce the derivation with different numbers. A useful mastery test is to
explain why each conjugate, normalisation factor and sign is necessary. Chapter 9 provides answer
checks, a solution workshop and a research protocol. Added derivation drills connect the algebra to
array indexing, circuit synthesis and QUBO compilation.
Scope. Forty pages cannot replace a semester of mechanics, complexity theory and optimisation. The
core derivations receive priority. Error correction, cryptographic security proofs and number-theoretic
success bounds are introduced with clear limits; the references provide the next course of study. No
claimed improvement to Athena is an experimental result.
Three questions to carry through the book
What mathematical object is being transformed? What can actually be measured? What does the
proposed speedup count, and what costs does it omit?

Self-contained lessons, original calculations, exercises with checks, and a reproducible optimisation design.

1.1 Complex numbers and phase
Source trail: [1], Lesson 1; [2], Lecture 3; [3], Chapter 2. References on p. 40.
A classical probability is nonnegative, but a quantum amplitude must also encode phase. Complex
numbers supply two real coordinates while supporting addition, multiplication and a length compat-

(1.1)
The angle 𝜃is measured from the positive real axis. Multiplying two polar forms multiplies their
lengths and adds their angles. This is why complex multiplication describes phase evolution so natu-
rally.
Euler’s formula 𝑒i𝜃= cos 𝜃+ i sin 𝜃follows by grouping the even and odd powers of the exponential
series. For a real or complex number 𝑤, this series is 𝑒𝑤= ∑∞

Because i2𝑘= (−1)𝑘and i2𝑘+1 = i(−1)𝑘, the two groups are the cosine and sine series. Setting 𝜃= 𝜋
gives Euler’s identity 𝑒i𝜋+ 1 = 0.
Worked example: Adding before squaring
Let two contributions to one output amplitude be 𝑢= 1/2 and 𝑣= i/2. Then |𝑢+𝑣|2 = |(1+i)/2|2 =
1/2. If instead 𝑣= −1/2, the result is zero. The magnitudes of the separate contributions are
unchanged, but their relative phase changes the answer.
In general,
|𝑢+ 𝑣|2 = |𝑢|2 + |𝑣|2 + 2 Re(𝑢∗𝑣).
(1.2)
The last term is interference. Re extracts the real part. It may be positive, zero or negative; the com-
plete squared modulus is always nonnegative. Contributions to the same outcome add as amplitudes.
Probabilities of distinct, mutually exclusive outcomes add as probabilities.
A state vector can be multiplied by a common phase 𝑒i𝛾without changing any probabilities. Indeed,
|𝑒i𝛾𝑧|2 = |𝑧|2. Relative phases between components survive this cancellation and are observable after a
suitable change of basis. Do not throw them away during a calculation.
Paper check. Find (1 + i)(2 −i) and |(1 + i)/2|. Answers: 3 + i and 1/√2. Explain why squaring
(1 + i)/2 itself does not produce a probability.
Derivation drill: normalise before measuring. For 𝑣= (1+i, 2)𝑇, compute 𝑣†𝑣= (1−i)(1+i)+4 = 6,
so |𝜓⟩= 𝑣/√6. The probabilities are 2/6 and 4/6. A phase i multiplying the entire vector changes
neither. By contrast, changing only its second coordinate changes its overlap with |+⟩. For the original
vector, ⟨+ ∣𝜓⟩= (3 + i)/√12, so 𝑝(+) = 10/12 = 5/6.
Try it first. Replace 2 by −2. The norm stays √6, but 𝑝(+) = |−1+i|2/12 = 1/6. The same computational-
basis probabilities can conceal very different interference. This is why a simulator must store complex
amplitudes until measurement.

A barren plateau is a training regime in which gradient variance shrinks exponentially with qubit num-

theorem that every quantum model is untrainable, nor does a nonzero analytic gradient guarantee it

If a typical gradient magnitude is order 2−𝑛/2 while shot error scales as 𝑆−1/2, resolving it at comparable
error can require 𝑆of order 2𝑛. Exact parameter-shift formulas do not remove this statistical cost. Noise
may suppress signal further. Gradient-free optimisers also need a distinguishable cost signal and are
not a universal cure.
Practical design responses include shallower circuits, local observables, structured initial parameters
and problem-informed ansatze. They are methods to test, not general guarantees. Increasing depth
can improve representational capacity while worsening noise and optimisation. Measure the tradeoff
rather than assuming bigger is better.
Worked example: A shot-budget sanity check
Suppose an observable has standard deviation near one and two parameter choices differ in expec-
tation by 10−3. With 𝑆= 104 independent shots the standard error is roughly 10−2, larger than the
difference. Order 106 shots are needed for a single-estimate error of 10−3, and reliable comparison
can require more. A small numerical loss change may be indistinguishable experimentally.
A sound hybrid learning loop is:
1. Fix data splits, input scaling, circuit family and measurement budget.
2. Estimate outputs and, when useful, gradients on training batches.
3. Update parameters with a classical optimiser and record total costs.
4. Select settings using validation data, then evaluate once on held-out tests.
5. Repeat across seeds; compare with classical models at matched budgets.
Quantum learning can have proven advantages for carefully specified access models or quantum-
generated data. These do not establish a broad practical advantage for classical text, ordinary tabu-
lar data or Athena’s intelligence. Claims require stating data access, output requirements, precision,
sample complexity and the best known classical alternative.

7.1 BB84: preparation, sifting and disturbance

Quantum key distribution (QKD) uses a quantum channel plus an authenticated classical channel to
establish shared secret key material. It requires devices that prepare and measure quantum states; ordi-
nary classical laptops alone cannot implement its physical security mechanism. A classical simulation
illustrates probabilities, not secure physical distribution.
In ideal BB84, Alice chooses a random bit 𝑎and random basis 𝑏∈{0, 1}. She sends H𝑏|𝑎⟩. Thus the four
states are |0⟩, |1⟩, |+⟩, |−⟩. Bob independently chooses a basis 𝑏′ and measures. Equal bases reproduce
Alice’s bit ideally; different bases produce a uniformly random bit because |⟨0 ∣+⟩|2 = |⟨1 ∣+⟩|2 = 1/2
and similarly for minus.
After receipt, Alice and Bob announce bases over the authenticated classical channel and discard mis-
matches. This sifting retains about half the transmissions for uniform independent basis choices. They
reveal a randomly chosen subset of retained bits to estimate the quantum bit error rate (QBER). The
revealed test bits are removed from potential key material.
Worked example: Intercept-and-resend produces a 25% sifted error rate
Suppose Eve intercepts every signal, measures in a random BB84 basis, and resends the state she
found. Conditional on Alice and Bob using the same basis, Eve chooses the wrong basis with
probability 1/2. In that branch Bob disagrees with Alice with probability 1/2. Hence the sifted
QBER is (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4. In an ideal independent model, 𝑚tested sifted bits all avoid an error
with probability (3/4)𝑚.
This calculation demonstrates one attack, not unconditional security. Eve may keep quantum memory,
entangle signals with ancillas, and wait for public announcements. A security proof must bound her
information under the specified device and channel assumptions.
No-cloning rules out making perfect copies of all four possible signal states. It does not forbid copy-
ing known orthogonal states, nor does it show that every measurement necessarily disturbs every
input. Security depends on incompatible possible preparations, statistical testing and post-processing

8.4 Evaluation, extensions and research hypotheses
A good optimiser minimises operational cost while returning feasible plans within a decision deadline.
Solver quality must be evaluated with the real business objective, not only its internal penalty energy.
Fix instance families, budgets, hardware and stopping rules before comparing methods.
Use exact enumeration on tiny cases to validate encodings; use matching for pure assignment and a
conventional mixed-integer or constraint solver for richer models. Add greedy plus local search as
a practical baseline and SA as the energy-based candidate. An optional annealer or QAOA backend
receives the same instances, with its embedding, parameter search and all repetitions included in the

9.2 Mini research challenge: can Athena allocate better?
Question. Can a quantum-inspired optimiser improve Athena’s task allocation compared with a con-
ventional scheduling algorithm? Formulate a narrow, falsifiable claim before implementing a backend.
Hypothesis. At a fixed end-to-end decision budget, SA with bit and feasible assignment-swap moves
reduces median feasible objective by at least 5% relative to greedy plus local search on held-out in-
stances with strong pairwise context costs, while maintaining at least 99% feasibility. These are pro-
posed targets, not results. A negative result is useful if the experiment can detect the intended effect.
Instance design. Generate task counts 8, 16, 32, 64, several agent counts, capability sparsity, capacity
limits, dependency density and pairwise-cost strengths. Construct feasible instances from a known
plan, then vary durations and costs. Separate assignment-only and scheduling families. Add recorded
workflows only when cost and duration definitions are consistent. Save every instance and generator
seed.
Baselines. Include exact enumeration for tiny encodings, optimal matching for independent unit-
capacity assignment, a conventional constraint or mixed-integer solver for scheduling, greedy with
a documented order, and greedy plus local search. The candidate is SA; optional quantum runs are
a separate arm. An exact solver can use its incumbent under the same timeout, while reporting an
optimality bound when available.
Variables and controls. Vary size, eligibility, interaction strength, prediction error and budget. Tune
temperature schedules, penalties and move types on training instances only. Hold out entire instance
families or workflow templates. Use multiple predeclared seeds, for example 30 per instance, and
budgets including model construction, decoding, repair and validation. Record failures instead of
deleting them.
Metrics and analysis. Report feasibility first, then cost gaps, decision-time distributions, deadline
misses, makespan and spend. Compare methods on the same instances. Bootstrap paired per-instance
differences to obtain a 95% interval; average repeated seeds within each instance first to avoid treat-
ing correlated repetitions as independent workloads. State the resampling method and show failures.
Report effect sizes and distributions, not only the best run.
Ablations. Remove pair costs; replace cooling with fixed-temperature search; replace bit moves with
swaps; warm-start methods equally. Separate benefits from a better model, starting plan and extra
compute. For quantum runs include network and queue latency, embedding, calibration, parameter
tuning and all shots; also preserve device-only timing for diagnosis.
Decision rule. Adopt the candidate only if the predefined quality target holds on held-out workloads
within the deadline and feasibility requirement. Otherwise retain the conventional method and docu-
ment where each solver works. A successful SA result establishes a classical engineering improvement,
not quantum advantage or improved general intelligence.
